mioc-016.title: Snakes boom in North America
mioc-016.text: Snakes had been a minor part of North American wildlife. In the Miocene their numbers and diversity rose sharply. Vipers and elapids, the cobra family, first appeared on the continent, and colubrids diversified into many modern genera. Snakes were among the animals that diversified as grassland spread, as {{ref:mioc-010}} describes.

mioc-022.title: Chiapas amber traps a Mexican forest
mioc-022.text: Resin from trees in Chiapas, Mexico, hardened into amber with life caught inside. It holds insects, other arthropods, plant fragments and even the fungi that grew on leaf surfaces. Together they make a fine-grained record of a Miocene forest.

mioc-028.title: Granites melt inside the High Himalaya
mioc-028.text: Deep inside the growing Himalaya, rock melted. Granites about 22 million years old intruded the High Himalayan Crystalline Sequence in many places. That metamorphic sequence is 30 km thick and forms the backbone of the range, holding its highest peaks. Many of these were leucogranites, pale granites melted from sediment-derived rock in crust thickened by collision.

mioc-029.title: New Zealand almost drowns
mioc-029.text: About 22 million years ago only 18% of present-day New Zealand stood above sea level. The rest lay under the sea, a stretch called the Oligocene Drowning Maximum. Isolation on scattered patches of land mattered for evolution. This drowning was very important in the radiation of the moa.

mioc-030.title: Tibet sinks, then rises again
mioc-030.text: The Tibetan Plateau did not climb steadily. Between 25.5 and 21.6 million years ago it sank about 900 m. Then, between 21.6 and 20.4 million years ago, it rose by 500 to 1,000 m, regaining much of the lost height.

mioc-031.title: Death at the Agate watering holes
mioc-031.text: In Nebraska, old watering holes became mass graves. Their deposits hold crowds of small rhinos that died together, along with bear dogs, entelodonts, camels and chalicotheres. The animals had gathered at the water, and many died there.

mioc-032.title: Lake Pebas floods western Amazonia
mioc-032.text: For millions of years, western Amazonia held a giant wetland. The Pebas Formation records this Pebas Mega-Wetland, or Lake Pebas, from about 21 to 8 million years ago. The formation covers about 1,000,000 square km. Its animals match those of La Venta in Colombia and Urumaco in Venezuela, tying the wetland into a wider northern South American world. Its end came as the Amazon took a new course, told in {{ref:mioc-099}}.

mioc-033.title: Conifers and cycads branch out
mioc-033.text: About 20 million years ago, some conifer and cycad groups began to diversify as conditions changed. These old seed-plant lines, far older than the grasses spreading around them, found new room in the shifting Miocene climate.

mioc-034.title: Rising rift shoulders split Africa's great rivers
mioc-034.text: Around 20 million years ago the western flank of the East African Rift rose. It cut the Great Lakes region off from the Congo basin. The map then looked very different. Lake Victoria did not yet exist, and Ethiopian and Ugandan rivers did not yet feed the Egyptian Nile.

mioc-035.title: Giraffes, hyenas and giant anteaters appear
mioc-035.text: Around 20 million years ago, three very different animals made their debut. The first giraffes, hyenas and giant anteaters all appear in the record at about this time. Bird diversity also increased, part of the Miocene's broad remaking of land life.

mioc-036.title: Arabia slams into Eurasia and the Tethys narrows
mioc-036.text: In the Early Miocene the Arabian part of Africa collided with Eurasia, cutting the Mediterranean off from the Indian Ocean. The first step of the closure, about 20 million years ago, cut water exchange by 90%. Two forces worked together. Africa-Arabia moved north, and sea level fell as the Antarctic Ice Sheet grew. By the mid-Burdigalian the collision had built a land bridge joining the two landmasses. The dates are contested. Sources place the Tethys closure anywhere from about 35 to 19-12 million years ago, and the two-step story used here, with the final step in {{ref:mioc-082}}, is one reading.

mioc-037.title: A land bridge sets animals crossing both ways
mioc-037.text: Gomphotheres and deinotheres, early relatives of elephants, were first out of Africa. They reached India by about 18.3 million years ago and Iberia by 18 million. Their road was a land bridge between Afro-Arabia and Eurasia, formed around 20 million years ago. Until then the open Tethyan seaway had kept most animals from crossing. The bridge set off the Great Old World Biotic Interchange, and traffic ran both ways. At least 37 Eurasian lineages entered Afro-Arabia during the Burdigalian. Perissodactyls reached Africa for the first time.

mioc-038.title: A gravity hole forms in the Indian Ocean
mioc-038.text: South of India, the sea surface sags. This depression, covering about 3 million square km, is Earth's largest gravity anomaly, and it formed around 20 million years ago. Models link it to plumes rising from a sinking slab of old Tethys seafloor, spreading low-density material beneath the Indian Ocean.

mioc-040.title: Southern Africa lifts and wears away
mioc-040.text: About 20 million years ago, southern Africa was lifted. That uplift began a long spell of erosion. Over the following millions of years, rivers and weather stripped away kilometres of rock from the raised land.

mioc-042.title: Most open-ocean sharks vanish
mioc-042.text: About 19 million years ago, roughly 70% of all open-ocean shark species disappeared. The seas that followed came to be ruled by large predators such as megalodon, met in {{ref:mioc-027}}, and the giant sperm whale Livyatan.

mioc-043.title: St Bathans, New Zealand's lost subtropical fauna
mioc-043.text: The St Bathans fauna of Central Otago, about 19 to 16 million years old, is New Zealand's only Cenozoic land fossil record. It holds early moa, kiwi and adzebills, tuatara relatives, crocodiles, turtles and many bats. Later cooling and drying wiped out its subtropical members.

mioc-041.title: Barstow's bones, teeth and footprints
mioc-041.text: In California, Miocene rivers and lakes laid down sediments between layers of rhyolite tuff, hardened volcanic ash. Those beds hold abundant vertebrate bones, teeth and footprints, and the ash layers help date them.

mioc-044.title: The Vogelsberg, Central Europe's biggest volcanic field
mioc-044.text: Central Europe's largest basalt formation covers about 2,500 km2 in Hesse, Germany. It is not one shield volcano but many overlapping volcanoes, built mainly in the Middle Miocene. Dates span 18.5-10 million years ago, peaking 17-15 million years ago. Its eruptions were tied to fault-block movement in the European Cenozoic Rift System.

mioc-045.title: The Ethiopian rift begins to unzip
mioc-045.text: The Nubian and Somali plates began to pull apart, and Ethiopia started to split. By one account rifting began about 18 million years ago at the south end, about 11 near the Afar and perhaps 8–6 in the centre. A study of the southern rift puts its start earlier, at 20–21 million years ago. Opening of the Gregory rift caused the Afar triple junction to form.

mioc-047.title: The Gulf of Suez rift reaches its peak
mioc-047.text: In the early Miocene the sea flooded the young Gulf of Suez rift, which then deepened. Rifting peaked in the Burdigalian, around 18 million years ago. In the Middle Miocene the Red Sea rift broke apart along its length, motion shifted to the Dead Sea Transform, and seafloor spreading followed.

mioc-050.title: Shanwang, where insect wings keep their colors
mioc-050.text: Over 600 species have come out of the Shanwang site in Shandong, China. The preservation is remarkable. Insects keep intact wing veins and even their colors, and the site also yields birds and mammals.

mioc-048.title: Iceland rises above the waves
mioc-048.text: Iceland sits where the Eurasian and North American plates pull apart, right above a mantle plume, a rising column of hot rock. That plume is thought to have built it. The island first rose above the ocean about 18-16 million years ago, and its oldest rocks formed above sea level date to 16.5 million years ago. The double setting gives it repeated volcanism and geysers.

mioc-046.title: Great apes and gibbons go separate ways
mioc-046.text: Somewhere between 18 and 12 million years ago, the line leading to great apes split from the line leading to gibbons. Molecular evidence, from comparing living species' DNA, places the common ancestor of the modern hominid group at 18 to 13 million years ago. The fossils are too scarce to name that ancestor. So this key branching point is known mainly from genes, not bones. The great-ape branch would later split again, as {{ref:mioc-137}} shows.

mioc-051.title: The Basin and Range begins to stretch
mioc-051.text: By the Early Miocene, most of the Farallon plate had been consumed beneath North America, and the Pacific-Farallon Ridge was nearing the continent. About 17 million years ago the crust in the west began to stretch. Tension thinned the land west of the Grand Canyon region and let it drop in blocks, carving a landscape of parallel ranges and basins. The movement has been large. Since extension began, parts of the province have shifted 60 to 300 km sideways, more in the south than the north.

mioc-052.title: Randeck Maar, a crater lake in a warm world
mioc-052.text: During the warm Miocene optimum, a crater lake in southwest Germany sat barely above sea level. Its sediments preserved plants, insects, fish and amphibians, a record of lake life in the warmest stretch of the epoch.
